3. That the present respondent No.1, as plaintiff, instituted Title Suit No.506 of 2009 before the 1St Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka against the present appellants for ejectment of the tenants, recovery of arrear rents and also for compensation contending, inter alia that his father got the suit property by lease from the then DIT (now RAJUK), who later on gifted it to his two sons, namely, the plaintiff-respondent No.1 and his younger brother Dr. Rafiq Ahmed(then a minor). The plaintiff-respondent No.1 after obtaining plan from RAJUK constructed a three-storied building thereon by spending his own funds as his younger brother was minor and inducted defendant-appellant as tenants therein upon entering into a tenancy agreement on 30.06.2003 for a period of 6 (six) years at a monthly rental of Tk.40,000/. In the said agreement, it was stipulated that if the tenancy agreement is not further extended beyond the stipulated period of six years, the defendants would hand over possession of the suit premises to plaintiff. In early 2009, the defendants stopped paying rents to the plaintiff and started depositing the rent with the House Rent Controller by filing House Rent Case No. 7 of 2009 in the 1st Court of Assistant Judge and House Rent Controller, Dhaka, under section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Act on the plea that one Dr. Rafiq Ahmed claiming to be the younger brother of the plaintiff asked for 50% of the rent to be paid to him and as such sought direction as to whom they would pay the rents. Thus the defendants became defaulters as per agreement. Consequently, on 26.05.2009 the plaintiff served Legal notice upon defendant No.3 terminating the tenancy agreement and asking them to pay the arrear rents, as well as to handover possession of the suit premises in his favour. In reply to the said notice, defendant No.3 stated that they are not ejectable tenants. Thus on 05.07.2009, the plaintiff again served another legal notice cancelling the tenancy agreement upon asking to handover possession of the suit premises, but they did not hand over the possession of the suit property in his favour. Hence, the suit. 

 4. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2(Spectra Catering Ltd. and Khan Md. Aftab, Chairman Spectra Catering Ltd) contested the suit by filing two separate written statements denying the material allegations made in the plaint. The defendant No.1 in its written statement contended, inter alia, that after taking 16ase it has invested Taka two crores for construction of a modern convention centre and have been paying rents to the plaintiff regularly. On 24.12.2008 Dr. Rafiq Ahmed, claiming himself the owner of half of the property issued demand notice upon the defendant to pay half of the rent to him. Under such situation the defendants filed Rent Case No. 7 of 2009 before the Rent Controller for determination as to whom the rents are to be paid. Till such determination they have been depositing rents with the Rent Controller. Therein the plaintiff filed an application for rejection of plaint which was rejected. It is further contended that the plaintiff has no requirement of the suit premises and the defendants are not defaulters in paying rents. 

 6. The trial court after hearing the parties and on consideration of materials on record decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 30.07.2012 and directed the defendants to hand over possession of the suit premises to the plaintiff and also to pay rent of TK. 40,000/- and cost of TK. 40,000/- per month to the plaintiff. Against the said judgment and decree the defendants preferred First Appeal No. 344 of 2012 before the High Court Division and the plaintiff also filed Cross Objection No.03 of 2013. A Division Bench of the High Court Division after hearing the parties dismissed the First Appeal and allowed the Cross Objection by judgment and decree dated 26.1.2014 with direction upon the defendant-appellants to pay the plaintiff-respondent No.1, Tk.40,000/- per month as rent and cost of Tk. 80,000/ per month as penalty from 01.01.2009 till their eviction from the suit property for their failure to hand over possession of the same to the plain-tiff-respondent No. 1. 

 7. In the meantime House Rent Case No. 7 of 2009 filed by the present appellants was heard and dismissed by judgment and order dated 16.1.2011 which was unsuccessfully challenged in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 26 of 2011 and then before the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3572 of 2011. A Single Bench of the High Court Division discharged the said Rule and affirmed the judgment and orders passed by the House Rent Controller as well as the learned District Judge, in the house rent case and in the miscellaneous appeal respectively, by judgment and order dated 18.7.2012. 

 8. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with all the aforesaid judgment and orders the present appellants preferred three Civil Petitions for leave to appeal before this Division and obtained leave in Civil Petition Nos. 585 and 592 of 2015, preferred against the judgment and order passed in the first appeal and the cross objection giving rise to the present two civil appeals. But Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 3107 of 2012, arising out of the House Rent case was not moved then. However, during the course of hearing the said two appeals, the Civil Petition was also taken up and heard and disposed of by this single judgment. 

 10. On the other hand, Mr. Mainul Hossein, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No.1 submits that the High Court Division committed no error in affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial court, because the defendant appellants by opening a new company named 'Spectra Convention Center Ltd.' stepped into the shoes of 'Spectra Catering Ltd.', the original tenant and in doing so it did not take consent from the land lord, the plaintiff-respondent. As a result, the defendant-appellant violated section 18(1)(b)of the Premises Rent Control Act. He next submits that during the continuance of the agreement and the tenancy the defendant-appellants stopped paying rents to the plaintiff-respondent (Landlord) and on the contrary they filed the rent case against the plaintiff and his brother Dr. Rafique Ahmed denying the ownership of the landlord. Moreover, the defendants also failed to pay the rents to the land-lord. As a result, the plaintiff-respondent served legal notice upon them to handover possession of the suit premises to the plaintiff-respondent No.1 which they failed to comply with and as such the tenancy agreement was cancelled before filing of the suit. Thus, the High Court Division was right in dismissing the appeal and allowing the cross objection imposing penalty upon the defendant-appellants. Thus, he prayed for dismissal of both the appeals. 

 11. On hearing the learned advocates for both the parties and on perusing the materials on record it appears that admittedly the lease agreement dated 30.6.2003 (Exhibit-1) was executed between the plaintiff respondent No.1 and one Major (Rtd.) Khalil. Bin Walid, Vice Chairman, Spectra Catering Limited. In clause 2 of the said agreement, it has been specifically mentioned that the contract is initially for 6 (six) years effective from 1.7.2003 ending on 30.6.2009 and in clause-3 it has been stipulated further that if both the parties agree it may be extended for another term of 6 years on fresh terms and conditions in a future agreement; in clause-5 of the said agreement, it was agreed that the lessee/tenant shall have to pull down all major modification works constructed/ erected on the premises and bring the demised premises to the original shape at its own expenses before leaving the demised premises on the expiry of the lease agreement; and in clause 7 it is contemplated that the lessor shall not have any right to put up a request to terminate the contract before expiry date (30.6.2009), provided that the lessee does not fail to go by its commitments/ obligations. In clause 8(ii) of the agreement the lessee was given permission to operate Spectra Convention Centre from the demised premises. In Clause 8(iv) the lessee was given a right to put up a request to the lessor for an extension of another term on negotiation in respect of the fresh terms and conditions of course such privilege was available only if the lessee be able to maintain good reputation/ credential with the lessor. But from the facts and circumstances as stated before it appears that the lessee defaulted to pay the monthly rents to the lessor from beginning of 2009 which was during the continuance of the agreement. Thus it is clear that they did not maintain good reputation/credential with the lessor during the continuance of the contract/ agreement and as such they have failed to go by their commitment/ obligations to pay rent regularly, nor they can avail the privilege of extension of the term on renewal of the agreement. So, both the Courts rightly found that the defendant-appellants have become defaulters and the termination of the contract by the lessor was lawful. 

 12. As regards to service of notice upon the defendant-appellants, it is claimed that no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, as required under the law, was served upon them. Perusing the materials on record it appears that the defendant-appellant stopped paying rents during the continuance of the agreement, from January 2009 and filed House Rent Case No.07 of 2009 before the learned Assistant Judge and House Rent Controller, Dhaka under section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Act. Due to such nonpayment of rents, the plaintiff-respondent No.1 served legal notice (Exhibit-3) upon the defendant-appellants wherein they were asked to pay the arrear rents and also his decision of cancellation of the agreement which was given effect from 1st July 2009. On 02.07.2009, the defendant-appellants replied to that notice (Exhibit-5) expressing themselves to be none-jectablc tenants. In the meantime, the tenancy agreement automatically came to an end on 30th June 2009, as the same was not Nctended or renewed by mutual agreement. Thus the plaintiff-respondent No.1 again sent another legal notice on 05.07.2009 asking the defendant-appellants to handover possession of the suit premises in his favour. But they did not pay any heed to such notice. From the above discussion it is clear that the plaintiff-respondent No.1 served proper notices upon the defendant-appellants which have been received and replied by the defendant-appellants. Moreover, according to clause-7 of the agreement the lessor (plaintiff-respondent No.1) has the right to terminate the contract, in case the lessees (defendant-appellants) fail to go by its obligation. As the defendant-appellants defaulted in paying the monthly rents in clear violation of the agreement, so the plaintiff-respondent No.1 committed no wrong in terminating the contract by serving notice upon them. Besides since the agreement was not renewed for further period, it met its natural death on the expiry of 6(six) years term on and from 1.7.2009. 

 13. The defendant-appellants claimed that on 13.12.2009 one Dr. Rafiq Ahmed, claiming himself to be the brother of the plaintiff-respondent No.1, served a demand notice upon them, claiming that he is the owner of half of the suit property, and directed them to pay 50% of the rent to him. As a result, they tried to communicate the plaintiff-respondent No.1 through a letter, but they failed to get any direction from him which constrained them to file House Rent Case No. 07 of 2009. Admittedly, the defendant-appellants entered into an agreement on 30.6.2003 with the plaintiff-respondent No.1 only admitting him as the landlord as so, they are to abide by the terms and conditions of the agreement and as such they cannot deny his title and possession over the demised property. By the said agreement (Exhibit-1) the appellants having admitted the respondent No.1 as the landlord and accordingly paid rents to him regularly till 2008, any doubt as claimed by him, has been removed. Thus the tenants/ lessees (appellants) are bound by their own admission in the agreement. Therefore, provision of section 19(2) of the Act of 1991 ceases to apply and thus it is the solemn duty on their part to pay rent directly to the landlord (respondent No.1). The appellants being tenants/lessees of respondent No.1 having not done so, the deposit, if any, made after 2008 to anybody other than the landlord is not valid tender of rent in law and as such the appellants have become defaulters. This view finds sup-port in the case of Abdul Layes Vs. Most. Anwara, reported in 29 DLR(S C) 13.Moreover, the tenants/ lessees (appellants herein) under such circumstances are estopped from denying the title and possession of the landlord (respondent No.1) under section 116 of the Evidence Act, which runs as follows: 

 14. Thus, it is clear that even if the lessees, (defendant-appellants), after due perseverance, failed to get any direction from the lessor, (plaintiff-respondent No.1), they cannot stop paying rents to him, raising doubt as to his ownership in the suit property. When a person enters into possession of an immovable property as a tenant admitting the ownership of the landlord, then neither he nor anyone through him shall be permitted, during the continuance of the tenancy, to deny the landlord's title however defective that title might be as has been decided by this Division in the case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Mohiuddin (38 DLR(AD)97), which has also been adopted in the case of Kasimuddin Mondol Vs. Jalaluddin Pramanik reported in 48 DLR(AD)205. 

 15. Now comes the question as to whether the High Court Division erred in allowing the cross objection and thereby imposing penalty upon the defendant-appellants. From the facts and circumstances of the case it is clear that the defendant-appellants not paying the rents in accordance with the agreement have committed an offence under section 26 of the Act of 1991. Under such circumstances considering the fact that the plaintiff has prayed for compensation in his suit directing to pay TK.80,000/- per month in addition to the rent of TK.40,000/- per month till vacating the premises cannot be termed unjustified. Thus, there is no illegality in the judgment impugned in the appeals, passed by the High Court Division. 

 16. As regards Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.3107 of 2012 filed by the lessees (defendant appellants) against the judgment and order dated 18.07.2012 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3572 of 2011 discharging the Rule and thereby affirming the judgment and order of both Miscellaneous Appeal No. 26 of 2011 and those of House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No. 7 of 2009 filed under section 19(2) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991, it appears that the lessees (present petitioners) filed the said rent case claiming that during the subsistence of the tenancy agreement Dr. Rafiq Ahmed, younger brother of the plaintiff-respondent No.1, served demand notice upon them claiming 50% ownership of the suit premises and accordingly demanded half of the monthly rents. Thus the present petitioners claimed that they were in doubt/confusion as to who was the real owner of the suit premises and to whom and how the rents are to be paid. From the materials on record it appears that the House Rent Controller as well as the other two higher Courts specifically found that the petitioners while depositing the rents with the Rent Controller specifically mentioned the name of the present respondent No.1 as the landlord and as such actually there was no doubt/confusion as to whom the rents were to be paid. The High Court Division in this regard considering the case of Alhaj Mir khan Vs. Alhaj Md. Rafiq Miah (13 BLD(AD)166) observed that 'since the tenants have acknowledged the opposite party No.1 as the landlord in the form for depositing the rents before the House Rent Controller, the said opposite party is entitled to receive the rents and as such the doubt/confusion as to whom and how the rents are to be paid does not arise at all'. Moreover, when there has been no dispute raised by any person claiming title of the demised premises nor there is any case pending before any Court or there is any decree of any Court or any deed of transfer in respect of the demised premises so there arises no question of any bona fide doubt/confusion as to whom the rents are to be paid. 

 17. In this respect it would be profitable to peruse Section 19(2) of the said Act which provides that: 'if the tenant has any bonafide doubt as to whom he would pay rents, then he can apply before the rent controller for permission to deposit monthly rents to it'. 

 18. The present defendant-appellants though claimed that one Dr. Rafiq Ahmed claimed 50% ownership of the suit premises but they failed to prove such claim by sufficient evidence as such they can-not deny the ownership of their landlord (the present respondent No.1) as decided in 29 DLR(SC) 13 (discussed above) and they are also estopped from doing so under section 116 of the Evidence Act as also discussed above. Moreover, if any dispute arises as to who is the owner of such premises, such dispute is to be disposed of/resolved by civil Court, not by the Rent Controller. Since the tenants/ lessees have acknowledged the present respondent No.1 as the landlord while depositing the rents before the House Rent Controller, it is clear that the respondent No.1 admittedly is the land-lord and as such, there is no bona fide confusion as to whom the tenants/lesse are to pay rents. Again when no rent was offered to the plaintiff-respondent No.1 prior to filing of the Rent case nor he having denied to accept the same, so the application under section 19(2) of the Act of 1991 is not maintainable in the present form and manner. Hence, the High Court Division was right in dismissing the Rule upon affirming those of the lower appellate court as well as those of the House Rent Controller.
